newsitem.title: FRANCE: Far-right poised to seize fourth French town.
newsitem.headline: Far-right poised to seize fourth French town.

text.p: Watched by the whole of France, voters in the depressed southern town of Vitrolles went to the polls on Sunday in a municipal election runoff which the extreme-right National Front looked set to win.
Victory in Vitrolles, north of Marseille, would take to four the number of southern town halls controlled by the anti-immigration Front, which is led by Jean-Marie Le Pen.
The runoff pits the outgoing mayor, Jean-Jacques Anglade of the Socialist Party, against Front candidate Catherine Megret, wife of the Front's number two, Bruno Megret.

Megret won 46.7 percent of the vote in last Sunday's first round, boosting the anti-immigration movement's score by four points since 1995. Her husband had been barred from running this time after a court found him guilty of campaign spending irregularities two years ago.
Anglade, who won re-election in 1995 by a mere 353 votes, took 37 percent last Sunday at the head of a united list of Socialists, Communists and ecologists on a 76 percent turnout.

Conservative candidate Roger Guichard scored 16.3 percent and pulled out of the second ballot at the insistence of Prime Minister Alain Juppe's centre-right national coalition, which urged a "republican vote to bar the road to the extreme-right".
Polls closed at six p.m. (1700 GMT) with turnout at 81 percent, a five-point jump on the first round but according to observers insufficient to allow Anglade to catch up with Megret.

Only a massive switch of centre-right votes to Anglade, and a strong turnout by those who stayed away from the polls in the first round, could stop the Front winning in Vitrolles, which has a population of 40,000.

"Who can say that the National Front is not capable of becoming France's first party? If you judge from the Vitrolles microcosm, you realise that it's possible," Le Pen told Europe-1 radio, adding that it would probably win a decisive victory.
Le Pen said that the French would come to realise "the shortcomings of those who lead them and...the failure to resolve major problems like unemployment, immigration, and taxes."
National centre-right leaders have stayed away from Vitrolles and it is far from certain their voters will switch to Anglade, whom they accuse of bankrupting the town.
If Megret wins, Vitrolles will be the fourth town to fall to the Front after a breakthrough in 1995 when it captured Toulon, Orange and Marignane.

Culture Minister Philippe Douste-Blazy, in a radio interview, urged centre-right voters to fight the Front "through militancy in the universities, unions, in daily life. If we're not capable of doing that, we'll be shattered."
Socialist chief Lionel Jospin and Communist leader Robert Hue, flanked by film stars and Jewish leaders, have appealed to Vitrolles citizens to vote against "racism and hatred".
But Socialist officials privately acknowledge that Anglade, under judicial investigation for alleged sleaze, is a poor advertisement for a party keen to shake off past graft scandals.

Bruno Megret, who plans to be his wife's chief aide if she wins, hammered home charges that France's political class is corrupt and told some 1,500 supporters at a final rally on Thursday their vote "impressed the whole of Europe".

The Front, which has played up the law-and-order issue in Vitrolles, advocates expelling some three million immigrants from France and giving preference in housing, jobs and welfare benefits to French nationals.
